items.title: Identifying Vertical Angles

sections.normalized_html: In the diagram above, two lines intersect at a point. If the measure of [MATH: \angle 1] is [MATH: 125^\circ,] what is the measure of angle [MATH: \angle 2?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/3aebc3dc0bb7f408685c3aafe5f2f379]

In the diagram above, two lines intersect at a point. If the measure of [MATH: \angle 1] is [MATH: 125^\circ,] what is the measure of angle [MATH: \angle 2?]

sections.normalized_html:
When two lines meet at a point, they create two pairs of opposite angles. The angles in each pair are called vertical angles. Vertical angles are always congruent.

In this case, angle [MATH: \angle 1] and angle [MATH: \angle 2] are vertical angles, so they have the same measure.

Therefore, the measure of [MATH: \angle 2] is [MATH: 125^\circ.]

[MATH: m^\circ + n^\circ + p^\circ = 180^\circ.]

[MATH: 60^{∘} + 70^{∘} + p^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; 130^{∘} + p^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; p^{∘}|= 50^{∘}.]

Therefore, the value of [MATH: p] is [MATH: 50.]

items.title: Using Vertical and Consecutive Interior Angles

sections.normalized_html: In the diagram above, lines [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] are parallel, and the line [MATH: w] intersects both. If [MATH: x = 2k + 14] and [MATH: y = 6k - 10,] what is the value of [MATH: z?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/4bfaaa5f173ca58394a18d3500bda247]

In the diagram above, lines [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] are parallel, and the line [MATH: w] intersects both. If [MATH: x = 2k + 14] and [MATH: y = 6k - 10,] what is the value of [MATH: z?]

sections.normalized_html:
From the diagram, we see that

  • The angles labeled [MATH: x^\circ] and [MATH: y^\circ] are vertical angles, so they are congruent: [MATH: x^\circ = y^\circ]

  • The angles labeled [MATH: x^\circ] and [MATH: z^\circ] are consecutive interior angles, so they are supplementary: [MATH: x^\circ + z^\circ = 180^\circ]

We are given expressions for [MATH: x] and [MATH: y.] Since [MATH: x^\circ = y^\circ,] we can write [MATH: (2k + 14)^\circ = (6k - 10)^\circ.]

Now, we solve for [MATH: k{:}]

[MATH: 2k + 14|= 6k − 10; 14 + 10|= 6k − 2k; 24|= 4k; k|= 6]

Substituting this value into the expression for [MATH: x,] we get

[MATH: x|= 2k + 14; = 2(6) + 14; = 12 + 14; = 26.]

Since [MATH: x^\circ] and [MATH: z^\circ] are supplementary, we have

[MATH: z^{∘}|= 180^{∘} − x^{∘}; = 180^{∘} − 26^{∘}; = 154^{∘}.]

Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: z = 154.]

[IMG: /graphics/d705a8db8be8d17625c20ac2aa821c0b]

In the diagram above, parallel lines [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] are intersected by the lines [MATH: p] and [MATH: q.] If [MATH: x = 40] and [MATH: y = 120,] what is the value of [MATH: z?]

sections.normalized_html:
We begin by examining the triangle formed by lines [MATH: p,] [MATH: q,] and [MATH: m.] This triangle has three interior angles:

  • One angle is formed at the intersection of lines [MATH: p] and [MATH: q.] This angle is vertical to the angle labeled [MATH: x^\circ,] hence, they are congruent. So, the measure of this first angle is [MATH: 40^\circ.]

  • A second angle is formed at the intersection of lines [MATH: p] and [MATH: m.] This angle lies adjacent to the angle labeled [MATH: y^\circ,] forming a linear pair. Since linear pairs are supplementary, the measure of this second angle is [MATH: 180^\circ - y^\circ = 180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ.]

  • The third angle is formed at the intersection of lines [MATH: q] and [MATH: m.] Since in any triangle the sum of the measures of its interior angles is [MATH: 180^\circ,] the measure of the third angle is [MATH: 180^\circ - 40^\circ - 60^\circ = 80^\circ.]

We can summarize these angles by adding them to the diagram, shown below.

Now observe the interior angle at the point where line [MATH: q] intersects line [MATH: n.] Since [MATH: m \parallel n,] and the line [MATH: q] acts as a transversal, this angle corresponds to the [MATH: 80^\circ] angle at the intersection of [MATH: q] and [MATH: m.] Since corresponding angles are congruent, the measure of this angle is also [MATH: 80^\circ.]

At the intersection of lines [MATH: q] and [MATH: n,] the two angles labeled [MATH: z^\circ] form a straight angle on [MATH: q] with the [MATH: 80^\circ] angle we just found. Since a straight angle measures [MATH: 180^\circ,] we obtain [MATH: z^{∘} + z^{∘} + 80^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; 2z^{∘} =|100^{∘}; z^{∘}|= 50^{∘}.]

Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: z = 50 .]
